Files to take apart

Drop video files or folders here Folders are searched completely.

What this does

Takes each file in the queue apart: a silent picture file plus every audio track and every subtitle as its own file, written next to the source. Your source file stays where it is and is not touched.

The details
  • Every track is copied exactly as it is: audio keeps its own format (.ac3, .dts, .eac3, .m4a, .flac …), subtitles stay untouched.
  • The silent picture keeps the source container — an MP4 stays an MP4, everything else becomes MKV.
  • Files with more than one track open a chooser, so you decide what gets pulled out.
  • No stereo mix here: a downmix would be a re-encode, and this route never re-encodes.
  • Nothing is cleaned up either, so Join can put it back together unchanged.
The details
  • The picture is copied, never re-encoded — it only loses its sound.
  • Audio is re-encoded to AAC wherever DaVinci would struggle: AC3, E-AC3, DTS, TrueHD, Opus, Vorbis and FLAC, anything with a layout other than mono, stereo or 5.1, and anything above 48 kHz. Everything else is copied as it is.
  • Text subtitles become cleaned-up .srt files; picture subtitles (PGS) are copied unchanged as .sup.
  • Files with more than one track open a chooser, so you decide what gets pulled out.
  • Audio with more than two channels can additionally be written as a stereo mix — it is in the chooser as its own line, and “keep all” does not include it.
There are no other options here — what the Convert page is set to makes no difference to either route.

Files to join

Drop whole batches here — video files plus their audio and subtitles They sort themselves into one job per film, by name. Dropping a folder adds the files inside it.

What this does

Builds a new MKV out of separate parts: a video file plus the audio and subtitle files that belong to it. Several films at once are fine — each video becomes its own job, and they run one after the other.

The details
  • The audio files you add replace the sound of the video file. Add subtitles only, and the video keeps its own sound.
  • Subtitles already inside the video file are never carried over — add them as files.
  • Your files stay where they are; the result is always a new file next to the video file.
  • What belongs together is decided by the name: everything that starts with the video's own name — the language endings Split writes are exactly that.
  • A job needs one video plus at least one audio or subtitle file. Groups that are short of that stay in the list and are simply left out.
  • Files in different folders are never mixed, even when they have the same name.
  • A .sub only works together with its .idx of the same name — drop both.
  • The converter names the result itself: it tidies the base name (spaces become dots) and picks another name if that one is taken.
The video can be .mkv .mp4 .m4v .mov — other formats cannot be used as a base here.

What this does

Keeps an eye on one folder and converts every video that turns up in it — on its own, without you dropping anything in.

No folder chosen yet.
What happens while this is on
  • Every video that turns up in that folder — or in any folder inside it — is converted on its own, with the options set below.
  • A file is only picked up once it has stopped growing for 30 seconds, so a download that is still running is left alone.
  • What is already in the folder when you switch on is taken along. Finished results and their sources are skipped, and so is the originals folder.
  • Watching only lasts while this window is open — closing it ends the standing order.
  • The results are written into an output folder next to their sources, and your originals are moved wherever your INI says. The watched folder will look different afterwards.
  • One video at a time here, whatever the Convert page is set to. This runs in the background, and the card still has to be free for the work you start by hand.

Options for the watched folder

Profiles are saved on the Convert page.
No “shut down when finished” here: a standing order that switches the machine off after the first video would never convert the second one. What each setting does is explained on the Convert page — the words are the same, only the choice is separate.

Settings — NVENCForge_Config.ini

Expert settings — safe to ignore, here for tinkering
Subtitle cleaner — the lines it throws away
Only when you take files apart for DaVinci. Split and Join never touch a subtitle, and an ordinary conversion does not clean either — so nothing here changes those. A phrase deletes every subtitle block it turns up in, upper or lower case makes no difference. Tick exact and a block only goes if it reads exactly like this and nothing else.
Changes apply to the next run; a run in progress keeps the settings it started with. The version before your last save is kept as NVENCForge_Config.ini.bak, and the state this program started with as NVENCForge_Config.ini.bak-<date_time> — that one is never touched again while the window is open.
Both figures along the bottom edge start again at zero — the space saved and the time spent.

Where it is

Updates

This window can fetch its own new releases. Nothing happens on its own: it asks GitHub only when you press the button. The version you are running now is kept as a backup in the tools folder, so there is always a way back. Updating is not possible while a conversion is running or a folder is being watched — a restart in the middle of a run would cut the converter off from its window.

NVENCForgeGUI is and stays free. The official source is on GitHub — anyone asking money for it is selling you what you can get there for free. Want to build it into a product that is not meant to be under the GPLv3? Ask the author for a separate licence.

What it is built on

  • Wails v2 (MIT licence) pairs the Go program with the WebView2 runtime Windows already ships. Wails stays under its own licence.
  • Go libraries — Wails and a handful of smaller ones built into the program — are under the MIT, BSD and Apache 2.0 licences, all compatible with the GPLv3. The README on GitHub names each one with its licence.
  • ab-av1 is a separate program by alexheretic under GPL-3.0. This window looks for it in its tools folder and fetches it from GitHub if it is missing.
  • FFmpeg (GPL build) does the actual encoding. ab-av1 needs ffmpeg/ffprobe on its path — this window downloads them into the tools folder on first run.

What it puts on your disk

Nothing is installed and nothing is written to the registry. Next to the program file there is only the tools folder. It holds the converter and FFmpeg, and three small files of its own: NVENCForgeGUI.window (size, place and whether it is day or night), NVENCForgeGUI.savings (space saved and time spent) and NVENCForgeGUI.profiles (your saved option sets). Delete the folder and it is gone — including the savings figures, so if you ever clear it out to fetch a fresh FFmpeg, those three files are worth keeping.

After an update there is one more file in there: the version you were running before, kept as NVENCForgeGUI-<version>.exe.bak. It is your way back — rename it to NVENCForgeGUI.exe and move it up one folder, and you are running the old version again. It is never deleted on its own, so if you do not want it, it is yours to remove.

Why it starts twice

Task Manager shows two NVENCForgeGUI entries, and that is meant to be. The Windows web view this window is drawn with sometimes stops while starting; when it does, the window is ended and cannot bring itself back. So the program starts once as a small watcher that holds no web view at all, and once as the window you see. If the window ever drops out, the watcher puts it straight back — twice at most — and closes the message for you. On the last try it leaves the message standing, so a lasting problem still says what it is. The watcher does nothing else: it writes no file and costs no start-up time worth measuring.

Buy the author a coffee

Both programs are free and stay free. If they have saved you a weekend of waiting — the bar along the bottom edge says how much — a coffee is a friendly way to say so. Entirely optional: nothing in the program is locked, limited or nagging without it.
